Using gross here would roughly halve the reported months in most European countries.

sources.notes: CONFIRMED from two official Dutch government sources, both fetched: (a) business.gov.nl, whose article is explicitly 'Published by: Immigration and Naturalisation Service, IND', and (b) government.nl, which names the full official instrument and its commencement date. Netherlands post-study job search: 1 YEAR. Official name: 'residence permit for the orientation year as a highly educated migrant seeking employment' (commonly 'orientation year' / Dutch 'oriëntatiejaar'); it came into effect on 1 March 2016. Confirmed benefits: free to work or start a business in the Netherlands for 1 year with no work permit (TWV) required; also permits starting a start-up. IMPORTANT SCOPE DETAIL for the corpus: eligibility is NOT limited to Dutch graduates. The government.nl page states the permit is intended for (i) foreign students studying in the Netherlands, (ii) foreign students who graduated from a top university OUTSIDE the Netherlands, and (iii) foreign scientific researchers who carried out research in the Netherlands — with application within 3 years of graduating. business.gov.nl adds that for study programmes completed outside the Netherlands the institution must be a 'designated international educational institution', i.e. top 200 of at least 2 of the main rankings (THE, QS, Shanghai) at the date of completion. This matters because a Bachelor-only graduate IS eligible (the IND form covers accredited bachelor's or master's programmes), unlike France where the equivalent permit is Master-level only. Confirmed limits: maximum 1 year, NOT extendable; a further orientation year can only be granted after a NEW completed study/research period after the previous permit expired; illegal overstay risks a Schengen entry ban. GAP: neither official page states the application fee amount; the IND fee (EUR 254, per the IND orientation-year application form) was seen only in search snippets and is NOT recorded as a claim here because I did not fetch a readable IND fee page. The IND's own orientation-year page (ind.nl/en/residence-permits/work/residence-permit-for-orientation-year) renders behind a nationality-input wizard, so its detailed condition list could not be quoted verbatim.

sources.notes: CONFIRMED from the immigration authority itself (IND), and the page is explicitly year-versioned as 'Required amounts 2026', so as_of = 2026. Netherlands financial proof for a study residence permit: EUR 1,130.77 PER MONTH for students at a university (or hbo) — covering courses of at least 2 years in duration, which includes Bachelor's-level study. This is the highest of the three countries researched (NL 1,130.77 vs DE 992.00 vs FR 877.50 EUR/month), a genuinely useful comparative finding. STRUCTURAL POINT: the Netherlands has NO German-style blocked account (Sperrkonto). The requirement is a monthly income threshold that must be evidenced, not a locked sum of money. The same IND page also publishes the two other thresholds directly relevant to a scholarship corpus, both recorded here: the ORIENTATION YEAR amount EUR 1,494.63 per month and the HIGHLY EDUCATED MIGRANT amount EUR 4,171.02 per month — the latter is a gross/monthly salary reference for highly skilled migrant sponsorship. Lower hbo bands (1-year: 892.88; 1+ year: 1,053.27) are recorded as context only. All amounts are month-1 figures for 2026 and are index-linked, so they must be re-verified each year.

sources.notes: CONFIRMED from the IND itself (page last updated 28 August 2026). Netherlands naturalisation: minimum 5 CONSECUTIVE YEARS lived in the Kingdom of the Netherlands with a valid residence permit. Official route: naturalisation, applied for via the municipality (gemeente) which forwards the request to the IND; a Royal Decree is then signed by the King and a naturalisation ceremony with a Declaration of Solidarity must be attended within 1 year of the positive decision or the nationality is not granted and a new application is required. CRITICAL POINT FOR THE CORPUS: the qualifying-permit list requires, at the time of application, during the procedure AND on the day of the ceremony, a permanent residence permit, a long-term EU resident permit, or 'A temporary residence permit with a non-temporary purpose of stay'. A Dutch study residence permit is a temporary permit with a TEMPORARY purpose, so it does not qualify on its own — the applicant must first hold a non-temporary status. Confirmed conditions: 18+, identity/nationality evidenced, always applied for extensions on time, civic integration exam passed at least at language level A2 (or exemption), not a danger to public order or national security, and generally must renounce current nationality (exemptions exist), plus the Declaration of Solidarity. IND decision period: 12 months. Language level required is A2 — materially LOWER than Germany's B1 and France's B1, which is a genuine comparative finding for the corpus. GAP: the IND page does not state the naturalisation application fee; it directs readers to a separate fees page I did not fetch, so no fee figure is recorded. The 'exceptions to the 5-year term' page for naturalisation was not fetched either.

sources.notes: CONFIRMED from the IND itself (page last updated 20 May 2026). Netherlands permanent residence: 5 CONSECUTIVE YEARS with a valid Dutch residence permit. Official name: verblijfsvergunning onbepaalde tijd ('permanent residence permit'), an unlimited-stay permit — 'A permanent residence permit has no end date', the document itself valid 5 years and renewable every 5 years. CRITICAL POINT FOR THE CORPUS: the requirement 'You now have a valid residence permit for a non-temporary residence purpose' means a student on a temporary study residence permit does NOT qualify at the moment of application — the 5 years must have elapsed AND the applicant must by then hold a non-temporary permit. Note also the interplay with the halving rule for study periods (see the companion exception file). Other conditions confirmed: main residence in the Netherlands for the whole 5 years; always extended on time; always met and still meets permit requirements; income requirements; BRP registration; civic integration exam passed at at least language level A2 (or exemption). Application fee EUR 254.00. The IND will first check whether the long-term EU resident requirements are met; if not, it will try to extend the current permit instead.

sources.notes: CONFIRMED from the university's own official fees page. Netherlands Bachelor tuition for non-EU/EFTA students at a public university: the University of Amsterdam charges an INSTITUTIONAL tuition fee of EUR 16,100 to EUR 19,900 PER YEAR for Bachelor's programmes. IMPORTANT HONEST LIMITATION: the UvA publishes a BAND, not a single figure, and states 'The amount depends on your nationality, where you are from and which degree programme you are enrolled in.' The exact amount is programme-specific and would require opening an individual programme page — I did not do that, so I must NOT collapse the band into a single number. For comparison, the same page gives EU/EFTA students EUR 2,694 per year for Bachelor's programmes, i.e. the non-EU/EU ratio at UvA is roughly 6x to 7x. Unit is explicitly per year (per the page: 'You will pay the tuition fee per year'). STRUCTURAL POINT FOR THE CORPUS: unlike France, where tuition is a national statutory tariff, Dutch non-EU tuition is an 'institutional tuition fee' set by each university individually, so there is no single Dutch non-EU Bachelor figure — any corpus value must name the institution and must not be presented as a national rate. GAP: the UvA page does NOT state a separate mandatory enrolment/student-society contribution, so no NL mandatory-fee figure is recorded from this source; I did not locate an official Dutch national mandatory-fee figure.
